blocks.text: Hydrology presented a different spatial problem because the observations changed through time as well as space. Rainfall, streamflow, groundwater levels and other measurements could be attached to gauges or other locations, but the processes being studied operated across catchments and along river networks. A catchment model therefore needed a geographic structure as well as a time series.

blocks.text: Sohail Afzal Choudhry’s 1998 University of Waikato doctoral research on the Kaimai hydropower project catchment provides a detailed New Zealand example. The work combined surface hydrological modelling with GIS and spatial time-series databases. ARC/INFO and ArcView were used alongside object-oriented programming and dynamic segmentation techniques. The research integrated catchment mapping, modelling and spatial time-series data within the same workflow.

blocks.text: GIS provided a way to organise the geography used by the hydrological model. Catchment areas, channels and other spatial components could be related to the measurements and parameters associated with them. Time-series records could then be connected to locations or sections of the network rather than treated as anonymous columns in a table. The model could use spatially varying information instead of assuming that one value represented an entire catchment.

blocks.text: Dynamic segmentation is one example of the technical work involved. A river line could carry changing attributes along its length without requiring every section to be redrawn as a completely separate feature. That approach was useful where measurements or model conditions applied to particular reaches. The technique also illustrates how scientific GIS moved beyond static overlay into more structured representations of processes that occurred along networks.

blocks.text: A multi-agency programme at the Whatawhata Research Station near Hamilton tested some of these questions on real land. Stream monitoring started in 1995, and an integrated catchment management group formed in 1996 with NIWA, AgResearch, Landcare Research, councils, farmers and Ngāti Māhanga representatives. The Mangaotama catchment was mapped and monitored alongside the Kiripaka and Whakakai comparison catchments. In 2000–2001 the project converted steep pasture to pine forestry and native restoration planting, changed livestock management and protected waterways. Monitoring stations, stream measurements, land-use classes, soils and farm economics gave the researchers a geographically specific way of testing the results. Whatawhata was a continuing field experiment, distinct from NIWA’s later national CLUES modelling application.

blocks.text: The Kaimai project was university research; NIWA also used GIS in its operational work. In October 2006 NIWA's Brent Wood described PostGIS running behind about half a dozen systems, with some datasets containing hundreds of millions of features. In December 2008 he described PostGIS, Apache and UMN MapServer as a standards-based web-mapping environment supporting WMS and WFS for maritime, fisheries, ecological and oceanographic work. By 2009 the same practitioner record included GeoServer and OpenLayers, and Andrew Watkins was working with GeoNetwork in 2010.

blocks.text: Between 2004 and 2006, NIWA led another application of GIS that crossed research-institute boundaries. A Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry and Ministry for the Environment project commissioned NIWA with AgResearch, HortResearch, Landcare Research, Lincoln Ventures and Harris Consulting to develop a catchment decision-support framework for estimating how land-use changes could affect water quality. The 2004 work proposed connecting NIWA's SPARROW catchment modelling with AgResearch's OVERSEER and HortResearch's SPASMO models through GIS. The 2006 Stage II report described the national, regional and catchment purposes of the framework and its intended computer-based tools. These are documented project aims and working stages, rather than proof that every proposed interface was ultimately delivered.

blocks.text: The multi-institute modelling programme produced a usable system called CLUES, Catchment Land Use for Environmental Sustainability. A later technical account dates its first release to 2005, while the July 2008 iEMSs paper describes the developed ArcGIS application and an early analysis of catchments at risk from nitrate sources. SPARROW modelled the river network and nutrient transport; OVERSEER and SPASMO contributed farm and horticultural nutrient estimates. A purpose-built control panel within ArcGIS handled catchment and reach selections, model runs, land-use scenarios and map or table output. By August 2009 a published evaluation recorded that regional council staff had been trained to use CLUES. Those dated accounts establish development, application and training beyond the proposed decision-support system described in the original 2004–2006 reports. Later ArcMap packages and newer model inputs belong to subsequent versions.

blocks.text: By the later 2000s, spatial databases and web services were ordinary production tools inside a national research organisation. They handled datasets at scales that would have been awkward to manage as map files alone, across applications used by different research units.
